big_idea: Fair shares means every plate gets the same. We deal one at a time until they are gone.
learning_intention: We are learning to share a small group of objects equally so every plate has the same amount.
student_learning_goal: I can share a small group of things equally onto plates so each plate has the same amount.
success_criteria: I can deal objects one at a time to each plate.
I can check that every plate has the same number.
I can tell what to do with leftovers.
lesson_specific_materials: Anchor chart 'Fair Sharing Rules' with 3 rows: (1) deal one at a time, (2) keep going until none are left, (3) check every plate has the same

OPTIONAL: Penny and Nick — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Lesson 4 formative tracker (Sharing Fairly) — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Penny baked 8 cookies. She has 2 friends. How can she share so nobody is sad?
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Hold up Penny and 8 paper cookies in a tray.

'Friends — Penny baked 8 cookies for the snack shop. Two of her friends came over: Nick and Quincy. Penny needs to share the cookies between her two friends so it's FAIR. What does fair mean?' Take responses. Listen for 'same' or 'equal'.

Confirm: 'Fair means every plate gets the SAME amount. So if I give Nick all 8 and Quincy zero, is that fair?' (No.) 'If I give Nick 6 and Quincy 2?' (No — different.) 'How can we share fairly?' Wait. Some children will say 'four and four'. Affirm: 'Yes — but how do we KNOW four is right? Watch.'

Place two paper plates on the carpet. Pick up cookies one at a time, alternating: 'one for Nick, one for Quincy, one for Nick, one for Quincy …' Continue until the tray is empty. 'Count Nick's plate. Count Quincy's plate. Are they the same?' Confirm 4 and 4. 'I shared fairly. I dealt them ONE at a time.' Add the rule to the anchor chart: DEAL ONE AT A TIME.
student_actions: Listen and watch the dealing demonstration.
Count each plate aloud after the share.
Read the rule 'deal one at a time' from the chart.

steps.instruction: Send children to small groups of 4. Each group gets 4 paper plates (M6) and 12 paper grapes (M7). Round 1: 'Share these 12 grapes fairly between 2 friends.' Children deal one at a time onto two plates. Check.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'You and your group are going to share 12 grapes between 2 friends. How will you make it fair? Tell me first.' Wait for 'one at a time'. 'Yes! When you finish, count each plate. Are they the same?' Visit each group to check. Expect 6 and 6.

steps.instruction: Round 2: 'Share 12 grapes fairly between 3 friends.' Children deal onto three plates. Check (4 and 4 and 4). Then ask: 'What was different about sharing for 3 friends versus 2?'
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Now 3 friends. Same 12 grapes. Share them fairly.' After dealing: 'Count each plate. Same?' (Yes — 4 each.) 'When there are MORE friends, each friend gets …' Wait. (Less.)

steps.instruction: Round 3 (the leftover round): 'Share 7 grapes fairly between 2 friends.' Children deal one at a time and discover one grape doesn't fit evenly.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Try this one: 7 grapes, 2 friends.' Children deal: 1-2-3-4-5-6 ends evenly at 3 and 3, then 1 grape is LEFT. 'Stop. What happened? You have one grape LEFT. Could you share that grape? Talk to your group.' Discuss: cut in half, give to teacher, eat together, set aside for later. There's no single 'right' answer; the discussion of fairness IS the point. Add LEFTOVERS to the anchor chart.

steps.instruction: Round 4 (stretch): 'Share 12 grapes fairly between 4 friends.' Each child should end up with 3. Have one child in each group be the 'fairness checker' who counts each plate at the end.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Last round. 12 grapes, 4 friends, including yourself. One person at your table is the FAIRNESS CHECKER — they count every plate at the end. Are they all 3? If not, fix it.' Walk around. Record on the tracker which children deal smoothly versus which need scaffolding.

steps.instruction: Class debrief: 'When was sharing easy? When was it tricky?' Lead the conversation toward LEFTOVERS as the trick — the one round that didn't share evenly is the most important one.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Which round was the hardest?' (Most kids: 7 grapes for 2 friends.) 'Why?' (Because of the leftover.) 'Yes — sometimes things don't share evenly. We have to TALK about what to do with the leftover. There's no one right answer, but everyone has to agree.'

differentiation.for_emerging: Reduce to 6 grapes for 2 friends and 8 grapes for 2 friends. Very small numbers eliminate counting fatigue and let the child focus on the dealing rhythm.
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch round: 'Share 15 grapes between 3 friends — but two friends are already best friends and want to share their plates together.' Introduces the idea of merged shares and challenges them to argue fairness when not all friends want equal individual shares.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Use a chant during dealing: 'one for you, one for me'. The verbal pattern matches the physical deal and builds the rhythm. Picture cards on the table show the rule visually.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Acted-out version: children stand in a circle and PASS the grape to the next person. The dealing rhythm is now embodied — the grape moves through the group rather than being placed onto plates.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Does the child deal one at a time (vs scooping piles)? Do they verify each plate has the same number after dealing? Can they articulate what to do with leftovers?
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the tracker per child as you circulate. The leftover-discussion column captures whether the child can EXPLAIN fairness, not just execute it.
tracker_columns: Deals one at a time (no scoop)
Checks each plate has the same

discussion_prompts: Can you tell me about a time you had to share fairly outside school?
Penny had 9 cookies and 3 friends. How would you share them?
What is the hardest part of sharing fairly?
consolidation.exit_routine: Each child whispers to a partner: 'If I had 10 things and 2 friends, each friend would get ___.' Partners check each other's answers, then walk to the wash-up station.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Sharing Fairly tracker for A6.9 (per-child observation across the 4 rounds), plus the completed worksheet 'Share It Fair'.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: A6.9 is a process expectation — fairness is conceptual, not arithmetic. Watching the dealing IS the assessment. Children who scoop piles instead of dealing one at a time are emerging; they may get the right answer by luck but haven't internalised the strategy. The leftover round (Step 3) is the diagnostic — children who can articulate what to do with the leftover own the fairness concept.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child scoops piles instead of dealing — repairing the fair-share strategy (Davis & Pitkethly, 1990; Mulligan & Mitchelmore, 1997; Empson & Levi, 2011)
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On A6.9 fair sharing, the most-documented K trap is the child who counts the total (12 grapes), counts the plates (3 plates), divides in their head (4 each), and PLACES 4 GRAPES at a time on each plate. It LOOKS like sharing, but it's actually a calculation followed by a mass-place — and it skips the dealing strategy entirely.

Davis & Pitkethly (1990) traced the development of partitive division strategies in K-G2 children and identified two distinct approaches: 'dealing' (one-for-you-one-for-me, reliable across leftover cases) and 'estimation-then-adjustment' (guess equal piles, then move grapes between piles to balance). They found the dealing strategy is the more robust K-appropriate tool — it handles every case including leftovers, scales to any number of recipients, and grounds later partitive division understanding.

Mulligan & Mitchelmore (1997) showed that K children who master the dealing strategy enter Grade 1 division with a working partitive schema, while children who rely only on mass-place fail when totals don't divide evenly. The leftover round (Step 3) is the diagnostic — children who can articulate what to do with the leftover own the fairness concept.

Empson & Levi (2011) build on CGI to show that fair-share problems are the K conceptual entry to fractions: leftover-fairness ('the leftover grape gets cut in half so each friend gets the same') is the seed of equal-partitioning. Validating leftover plans rather than rejecting them protects this trajectory.

Why this matters: when this child encounters a leftover round (7 grapes for 2 plates), they freeze because their calculation strategy can't handle uneven numbers. The dealing strategy ('one for you, one for me') handles every case, including leftovers. Step 1 (Round 1, 12 grapes for 2 friends) is where the trap shows up — the child mass-places 6 on each plate and is satisfied. Without intervention, they will fail Round 3.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Round 1 just started. The group of four children has 12 paper grapes and 2 paper plates. One child (call him Sam) has scooped 6 grapes in one motion and placed them on Plate A, then scooped the remaining 6 and placed them on Plate B. He looks up: 'Done!' He is correct mathematically but used calculation, not dealing. The teacher steps in BEFORE Round 2, while the strategy can still be coached.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch beside Sam. 'Tell me how you shared.' He says '6 and 6'. 'How did you know?' (I counted 12 and split in half.) Affirm: 'Great math thinking! But I want to teach you another way. Sometimes we don't KNOW the answer ahead of time — like when we have 7 and 2 friends.' Watch his face. 'Try this round again, but this time deal ONE grape at a time. One for Plate A, one for Plate B, one for A, one for B. Don't think about the total; just keep dealing until the tray is empty. Then count each plate.'

Mix up the grapes. Watch Sam deal. He'll be slower this time but will end up at 6 and 6. 'See? Same answer, different STRATEGY. The dealing strategy works EVERY time, even when the answer isn't obvious. Wait until Round 3 and you'll see why.'

Round 3 arrives: 7 grapes, 2 plates. Sam now deals one at a time naturally. After 6 deals (3 on each plate), one grape is left. He pauses. 'See?! The dealing strategy SHOWED you the leftover. If you'd guessed and split — you might have given Plate A four grapes and Plate B three. The dealing told you the truth.' Tick 'deals one at a time' on the tracker.

This is the long-term recovery move: the dealing strategy is the K-appropriate tool. By Grade 1 these children will learn division and mental partitioning, but not yet. Right now the goal is fluency with the deal.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Scoops uneven piles and places them anywhere. Makes no attempt at fairness. Hasn't connected dealing to equal shares yet.
(Mid) Scoops EQUAL-LOOKING piles in one motion, then visually checks. Gets right answer when totals share evenly; freezes on leftover rounds.
(Strong) Deals one at a time naturally, checks each plate at the end. Articulates 'one for you, one for me' as a rule.
(Stretched) Voluntarily explains: 'I dealt because I didn't know how it would come out. The dealing told me what each plate got.' Has internalised the strategy AS a strategy, not as a procedure.
common_misconceptions: Sharing means splitting in half. (Child only knows how to share between 2 friends — freezes at 3+ friends.)
Leftovers mean someone gets more. (Child mistakenly gives the leftover to one friend, breaking fairness.)
Sharing means counting total then dividing. (Child's calculation strategy works for some cases but fails on uneven shares — the dealing strategy is more robust.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child mass-places (Davis & Pitkethly's 'estimation-then-adjustment'): always have the child say the chant aloud while dealing — 'one for you, one for me, one for you, one for me'. The verbal rhythm prevents scooping. Repeat this on Round 2 BEFORE the leftover round to build the rhythm before the diagnostic.

DIAGNOSTIC B — child handles even rounds but freezes on the leftover round (7-for-2): use the leftover AS the teaching moment, not as a fail. Pause the group; ask 'what should we do with the leftover?'; let the group propose (cut in half, save for later, give to teacher). All proposals are valid (Empson & Levi's equal-partitioning seed) — the FAIRNESS lives in the agreement, not in the procedure.

DIAGNOSTIC C — child gives the leftover to one friend (breaks fairness, doesn't yet see the agreement requirement): physically pause; have the child re-deal from scratch with the leftover anticipated; ask 'is everyone happy?' before any plate is touched again; only mark the round complete when every friend says yes. Fairness as social agreement is Mulligan & Mitchelmore's K-appropriate framing.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of A6.9 — sharing a small group equally onto plates and reasoning about leftovers.

parts_outline.task: Three sharing scenes printed on the page. Scene A: 8 cookies, 2 plates — child draws cookies onto plates. Scene B: 12 grapes, 3 plates. Scene C: 9 stickers, 3 plates. The child draws each share and writes how many on each plate.
Two leftover scenes. Scene A: 7 cookies, 2 plates. Scene B: 10 grapes, 3 plates. The child draws the share, circles the leftover, and writes a one-sentence plan for what to do with the leftover.
Empty 'My Sharing Story'. The child draws their own scene: how many things, how many plates, the share. Sentence starter: 'I shared __ between __ friends. Each friend got __.'
